summary: Takes al-anfal to mean the spoils of war, and reads the verse as placing them wholly at the disposal of Allah and His Messenger to allocate, citing for this a report from Ibn 'Abbas transmitted by al-Bukhari. The consequence drawn is that no individual fighter held a claim of his own on what had been taken: the disposal of it was never theirs to settle between themselves.

Reads the verse as setting one unease beside another. The believers' discomfort at the ruling on the spoils is paralleled with a discomfort of the same kind they had felt earlier, when they were commanded out from their homes toward the Quraysh army rather than the caravan they had expected to meet.

Glosses "brought you forth from your home" as the departure toward Badr, and supplies the occasion briefly: Abu Sufyan's caravan got away, and Abu Jahl mobilised the Quraysh in response, so the encounter that followed was not the one the march had been aimed at.

Gives the Prophet's supplication for help as the direct occasion of the verse, citing the report this graph already carries as muslim:1763. Alongside it, and separately, records al-Miqdad's declaration of loyalty to the Prophet made before the fighting began.

Reads the verse as the plea for help and the answer given to it: a reinforcement of a thousand angels, arriving rank behind rank rather than all at once. Notes a variant reading on which "a thousand" is read as a plural, "thousands", and observes that the number is raised in the later passage at 3:124-125.

Frames the verse as a correction of self-credit: neither the killing nor the throwing was truly the believers' own doing, however much the day had gone their way. Read this way the verse is aimed at the pride a victory invites, withholding the achievement from the ones who might otherwise claim it.

Parses the grammar of the negation followed by the affirmation — "you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw". The two are not a contradiction: the act is ascribed to Allah, and the Prophet's physical motion is not what the negation literally denies.

Ties the ruling of the verse to the ransom that was taken for the captives of Badr. Records separately, on a report transmitted by Abu Dawud, that the ransom was fixed at four hundred dirhams for each captive.
States that the verse was revealed specifically regarding the ransoming of the captives taken at Badr, and notes that its ruling was later understood to have been modified by a subsequent verse.

Reads the verse as the command given to the Prophet to rouse the believers to fight, and takes Umayr ibn al-Humam as the illustration of what answering that encouragement looked like: hearing what was promised, he threw away the dates he was still eating as too long a thing to wait for, and went forward into the fighting rather than hold on for a long life.

Gives the verse's occasion as the single combat that opened Badr — three men from each side — and cites al-Bukhari's own tafsir for the identification. Quoted there is Ali's statement that he is the first who will kneel before the Merciful to have this dispute settled on the Day of Resurrection, so the two contending parties the verse describes are read as the two sets of three who fought.

Cites al-Bara' ibn 'Azib's report — the one this graph already carries as bukhari:3957, recorded by al-Bukhari — that those who came out to fight at Badr were a little over three hundred and ten, and sets that number beside the number who crossed the river with Talut and held with him. The comparison is what the episode is read for: the smaller party overcame the larger by Allah's leave, so what settled the day was the help that came from Allah and not the count of the men who fought.
